episode_title: Building a Work Culture of Discipline and Calm with Stephen Callender of Foster Commerce

real_qa.q: How does Foster Commerce break down large projects into smaller tasks for engineering teams?
real_qa.r: Foster Commerce breaks large projects into smaller chunks that are measurable and concrete. The team ensures that tasks are no more than eight hours at a time, with all huge projects ultimately broken down into smaller and smaller units. This approach includes extensive prep work, spec notes, and frequent check-ins so that developers cannot go a week without communicating what they are working on.

real_qa.q: What is Foster Commerce's policy on real-time messaging and interruptions in the workplace?
real_qa.r: Foster Commerce does not use Slack purposefully because it is an interruption machine. The expectation is that team members will receive a response by tomorrow, not immediately. Interrupting someone is not allowed; it requires privilege and power that is deliberately not granted. This policy applies across all team members to protect deep work time.

real_qa.q: How does Stephen Callender implement daily self-reports instead of constant check-ins?
real_qa.r: Foster Commerce uses regular daily and weekly self-reports where developers document their progress and status. This institutionalized process provides the information needed without interrupting them throughout the day. The team has a specific pattern for these self-reports that has been set up and integrated into their workflow, allowing Stephen to know project status by reviewing notes rather than asking developers directly.

real_qa.q: What happened when Foster Commerce did not implement strict project oversight early on?
real_qa.r: Stephen hired a developer, gave him a project with a deadline, and checked in only at the end. After two months, when it came time to deliver, the work was completely wrong and unusable. This experience forced Stephen to institute regular check-ins and ultimately led to the daily self-report system and eight-hour task limits that define Foster Commerce's current approach.

real_qa.q: How does Foster Commerce apply the principle of planning only to the level of visibility you have?
real_qa.r: Foster Commerce plans only for what can be clearly seen right now rather than trying to plan months ahead. When a developer receives a large assignment, they first write an implementation method—their plan for how they will tackle it. If they cannot plan beyond a certain point without seeing feedback from their own code, that is acceptable as long as they commit to check-ins at defined intervals like four or eight hours.

real_qa.q: What phrase from military discipline does Stephen Callender apply to Foster Commerce's methodology?
real_qa.r: The phrase 'slow is smooth, smooth is fast' is central to Foster Commerce's approach. Stephen uses this Navy SEALs principle to explain the methodology: slow down to make sure the road ahead is smooth and plan it out, and then moving forward becomes easier. This philosophy is reflected in the emphasis on prep work, spec notes, and thorough planning before execution.

guest.bio_context: Stephen Callender is the owner of Foster Commerce, a custom development agency specializing in web apps and websites. He has extensive experience managing engineering teams and has developed a distinctive approach to project management and team discipline that prioritizes clear specifications, task breakdown, and frequent communication to prevent costly project failures.

key_stats: Eight hours: maximum task duration for any developer at Foster Commerce
Weekly planning cycles: Foster Commerce creates a new plan for every single person each week, not beyond
One major project failure: Stephen hired a developer without weekly check-ins; after two months the entire work was unusable and had to be rewritten
